title: Ageing and style terms
subtitle: Words that tell you more
objectives: Explain Spanish and Italian ageing terms
Recognise terms with no legal meaning

steps.title: Ageing terms
steps.body: Some terms set minimum ageing. In Spain, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva each require more time in oak and bottle; Rioja Gran Reserva reds need at least five years, with two in oak. In Italy, Riserva means longer ageing than the standard wine, with rules set for each DOC. Portugal's Reserva requires higher alcohol and quality approval.

steps.title: Sweetness terms
steps.body: Sparkling wines use a scale based on grams of sugar per litre: Brut Nature up to 3, Extra Brut up to 6, Brut up to 12, Extra Dry 12 to 17, Dry 17 to 32, Demi-Sec 32 to 50, Doux over 50. Still wines use terms like sec, demi-sec, moelleux and doux in France, or trocken and halbtrocken in Germany.

steps.prompt: Which sparkling wine term means the driest of these?
steps.explanation: Brut, up to 12 g/l, is drier than Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l. The naming is confusing but legal.

steps.title: Words without rules
steps.body: Many attractive words have no legal meaning in many countries: Reserve outside Europe, Old Vines, Natural and Premium. Organic, by contrast, is regulated: certified organic wine must follow rules on farming and winemaking, including lower sulphur limits in the EU.
steps.highlight: Organic is regulated; Old Vines usually isn't

steps.prompt: Which terms have a legal ageing meaning in Spain?
steps.explanation: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are regulated. Old Vines has no legal definition.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spanish and Italian terms like Reserva and Riserva set minimum ageing
Sparkling sweetness terms follow a sugar scale, with Brut dry
Many attractive words, like Old Vines, have no legal meaning
